articles.text: Final part in 7-part series The Post concludes its candidates’ questionnaire series with one final question posed to candidates for City Council. Each week a question was sent on Thursday to the four candidates with a request to limit answers to 200 words. Week 7 Question: Piedmont has very little commerce. Would you support encouraging some new business in the city? If so, please be specific on the location and type of businesses you would like to see? Lorrel Plimier, Candidate Yes, I support encouraging new business in Piedmont. I believe that businesses here should meet the needs of and foster community among our residents. I also believe it’s very important to continue to get community input when discussing changes to Piedmont’s by-right permitted commercial uses. I don’t support expanding our current commercial zoned area, without a vote of the residents to approve this change. We have 13 parcels zoned for commercial use along Grand Ave between Wildwood and Linda. Located on these lots are Ace Hardware, the Shell station that is under transition, a new beauty salon, medical and dental businesses, as well as five single family homes. Another six parcels are zoned for commercial use in the city center. This is where Mulberry’s, three banks, a real estate office, and the gas station are located. I think the commercial parcels could be more effectively used and I support thoughtful, strategic planning to evaluate the use. The city center is especially important for the vibrancy of our community. Plenty of problems with Shell Recharge proposal The following letter was sent to the Piedmont Planning Commission. Editor: I live at 1250 Grand Avenue, across the street from Ace Hardware and one house north of 29 Wildwood, on Grand Avenue. I’m pleased about the overall direction for 29 Wildwood; the EV hub is very promising. We appreciate the effort that Shell Oil and the Planning Commission have executed towards developing the plans. Unfortunately, I have not seen any discernible impact of the input from myself and affected residents on those plans. I will repeat the input here, and offer some solutions. The primary and consistent objection is the 24/7/365 operating hours, with attendant disturbances of noise and safety/security. 24/7/365 operating hours creates an actual and attractive nuisance. There is ample evidence of increased crime related to EV charging stations. 24/7/365 operating hours creates undue noise, invites loitering, and puts the burden of monitoring and supervision on neighbors and residents. The basis of Staff recommendations is the Initial Study prepared by LSA. The Initial Study is misleading regarding the change in site intensity, and Staff report repeats the misdirection. The Staff report quotes the Initial Study as to a reduction of 123 daily trips. This is based on an over-characterization of daily trips for the site as a gas station, and under-characterization of the intensity of usage as an EV hub. Table 4.17.8 “Trip Generation Comparison” on page 102 supposes that the gas station was generating 688 average daily trips (gross). With a five minute fueling time, this would require that each of the four hoses to have been in continuous use for 14.3 hours per day. The same table similarly undersells the EV daily average trips. The table supposes there will be 468 EV average daily trips (gross). With a 30 minute charging time, this would allow for the 14 chargers to be in continuous use for 16.5 hours per day. articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation and its Community Engagement Committee invites the public to a reception at Piedmont High School on Thursday, November 14, starting at 5:30 p.m. Piedmont’s highly regarded schools are a key draw for many residents. Even people without children in the district are attracted to the area because they align with a community that values education. Rich and Barbara Thompson were empty nesters drawn to Piedmont in part for its reputation for excellence in its public schools. They also realize that civic engagement is not only personally rewarding but critical to the success of the community. With this mindset, Rich joined the Piedmont Education Foundation Board in 2020 and this year is chairing the foundation’s Community Engagement Committee which includes Molly Lloyd and Sarah Pearson. “I want to make sure that other members of the community, who don’t currently have students in the district, have a chance to learn more about our schools firsthand,” said Rich. The first of several events planned for this year is the reception on November 14. School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn will provide an update on the district, and community members will have a chance to enjoy our beautiful school facilities and mingle with some current school leaders. “We are excited to reconnect with fellow empty nesters at the reception,” said Katherine Campbell. “We had three children graduate from PHS and are so thankful. Whether we were watching our children on stage, the football field or in the pool playing water polo, we are grateful for all of the great experiences.” To RSVP for the reception, click on: paperlesspost.com/ go/5BAe905hjLbyVahLwQd23. Following the reception, all are welcome to watch the PHS fall play, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, which begins at 7 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. articles.text: Final part in 7-part series Candidates for Piedmont’s school board received one final query from the Piedmont Post this past week. Candidates were asked to limit their answers to 200 words. School Board 3 open seats; 3 candidates. Question Traditionally, the top vote getter is on track for the role of school board president, after current board members. If Piedmonters only had one vote, instead of three, why should they vote for you to be on the school board? MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate I’m running for school board to help deliver better outcomes for our students, staff, and community. As such, I’m not concerned about titles, but rather what we actually accomplish together. With that in mind, here’s what I hope to achieve over the next four years: As a member of the Board of Education, I will work tirelessly to ensure your student receives a solid education in a diverse, open, and welcoming environment. Every Piedmont student is unique – each has different interests, gifts, and goals, which often change as they grow. Consequently, I believe our district must meet each student where they are, and challenge them appropriately, as much and as soon as they’re ready. I support innovation in teaching and curriculum, but ultimately what matters is the quality of outcomes for our students. My position on curriculum calls for subject matter depth, with more direct exposure to and practice with foundational content, accessible to each and every student. I stand with Max and Susy on fiscal responsibility and getting us to a workable and sustainable budget. If this resonates with you, then I’d be honored to receive your vote, as a tangible affirmation of the vision I’ve expressed. SUSY STRUBLE, Candidate A key reason to vote for me for school board is because I bring a thoughtful, organized, and community-focused approach to problem-solving—an approach that’s essential for addressing important challenges and opportunities in our district. I frame problems clearly and collaborate effectively to find solutions that are both practical and impactful. However, I believe it’s a benefit to Piedmonters that they have more than one vote in this school board election. Over the past few weeks, Michael, Max, and I have dived more deeply into key district topics through community forums and district meetings. We’ve gotten to know each other better, and with each conversation, I’m even more excited about the value we will bring. Our knowledge, skills, and approaches differ but are complementary, and we each have connections in different Piedmont communities. This short time together has been incredibly productive, and I look forward to joining the existing board members to help serve the Piedmont community. MAX ROMAN, Candidate I truly believe that all five of us will make a great team, with varied experiences and expertise that we can use for the benefit of our kids. In my years on other boards, both corporate and nonprofit, I find there is often a disconnect between ideas and action; people often get stuck debating. Where I think I excel is in distilling ideas and feedback from multiple sources into actionable items that can make real change, and I look forward to doing that for our schools. Additionally I think my perspective as someone who grew up in Piedmont, attended and graduated from Piedmont schools, with a parent who worked in our district, is a valuable one. Michael Malione Max Roman Susy Struble

Question Traditionally, the top vote getter is on track for the role of school board president, after current board members. If Piedmonters only had one vote, instead of three, why should they vote for you to be on the school board? MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate I’m running for school board to help deliver better outcomes for our students, staff, and community. As such, I’m not concerned about titles, but rather what we actually accomplish together. With that in mind, here’s what I hope to achieve over the next four years: As a member of the Board of Education, I will work tirelessly to ensure your student receives a solid education in a diverse, open, and welcoming environment. Every Piedmont student is unique – each has different interests, gifts, and goals, which often change as they grow. Consequently, I believe our district must meet each student where they are, and challenge them appropriately, as much and as soon as they’re ready. I support innovation in teaching and curriculum, but ultimately what matters is the quality of outcomes for our students. My position on curriculum calls for subject matter depth, with more direct exposure to and practice with foundational content, accessible to each and every student. I stand with Max and Susy on fiscal responsibility and getting us to a workable and sustainable budget. If this resonates with you, then I’d be honored to receive your vote, as a tangible affirmation of the vision I’ve expressed. SUSY STRUBLE, Candidate A key reason to vote for me for school board is because I bring a thoughtful, organized, and community-focused approach to problem-solving—an approach that’s essential for addressing important challenges and opportunities in our district. I frame problems clearly and collaborate effectively to find solutions that are both practical and impactful. However, I believe it’s a benefit to Piedmonters that they have more than one vote in this school board election. Over the past few weeks, Michael, Max, and I have dived more deeply into key district topics through community forums and district meetings. We’ve gotten to know each other better, and with each conversation, I’m even more excited about the value we will bring. Our knowledge, skills, and approaches differ but are complementary, and we each have connections in different Piedmont communities. This short time together has been incredibly productive, and I look forward to joining the existing board members to help serve the Piedmont community. Where I think I excel is in distilling ideas and feedback from multiple sources into actionable items that can make real change, and I look forward to doing that for our schools. articles.text: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will perform The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time for their Fall play. The play will come to life in three showings Thursday to Saturday, November 14-16, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. Fifteen-year-old Christopher Boone lives in Swindon, a quiet working-class town on the outskirts of London with his single father. After Christopher’s neatly structured world is sent unraveling by the death of his neighbor’s beloved dog, he embarks on the adventure of a lifetime. This powerful drama weaves together the excitement of mystery and adventure as well as heartwarming and heartbreaking aspects of love, trust, and family as Christopher’s investigation alters the course of his life. This production of The Curious Incident is Simon Stephen’s abridged theatrical adaptation of Mark Haddon’s 2003 best-selling novel, which was translated into 44 languages and sold more than 5.5 million copies worldwide. The first production in 2012 in London’s West End, won seven Olivier awards including Best Play. articles.text: On a blistering hot October day, seven Troop 1 Scouts and two adults set out to bike eight miles up 1,400 feet of vertical to reach Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland hills. At the start of the trip they loaded camping gear into a car so that they only had to bike with a light day-pack with lunch, snacks, and water. The first four miles were easy, mostly downhill and flat; however it soon became steep. They stopped at Lake Temescal for snacks and soaked their shirts in the water to cool off The last four miles were a slow, steep climb up the winding hills. They stopped frequently to rest and rehydrate in the 93 degree heat. The climb was not without rewards though. There were breathtaking views of virtually the whole Bay stretching for miles. When they reached the apex of the climb they were rewarded with a short stretch of downhill riding to the entrance of the park. Their camping gear arrived shortly after by car taking only 15 minutes to do what took almost three hours by bike. After enjoying popsicles, they grabbed their gear and mustered some remaining energy for the short but steep hike to the campsite. After setting up the campsite, while the adults relaxed, most of the Scouts picked up their bikes to zoom around the dirt trails throughout the park. In late afternoon they went on a walk to explore one of the labyrinths in the park. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team glided through the first round of the Western Alameda County Conference playoffs with a 14-9 thrashing of Bishop O’Dowd on Monday, October 29 at the Encinal Pool in Alameda. The Highlanders face top seed Berkeley in the semifinals today, October 30. After ending the first quarter in a 2-2 tie with O’Dowd, PHS exploded for five goals in the second quarter while allowing two. Both teams added two goals in the third quarter, while the Highlanders poured on seven goals in the fourth. “Credit where it’s due, their goalie had a good game. We didn’t execute our 6-on-5, partly due to their defense. But in the third and fourth quarters, all the work we did drawing ejections paid dividends when we started getting mismatches,” explained John Savage, who has returned as head coach this fall. “We start a little slow sometimes and just have to come out with more intensity. We had a lot of opportunities in the first two quarters, but we improved as the game went on,” said junior Elles Kreickhaus. With a 13-8 overall record, Piedmont enters the WACC Tournament as the No. 4 seed. “We’re humming. We’re starting to see what we’ve been preaching – where to work the ball,” Savage said. “We’ve built a lot of chemistry as the season has gone on. The last two years we had George Stein and Declan Linnane really leading the way. Now, it’s more balanced. Everyone needs to do their part,” Kreickhaus said. Making an impact this year is freshman Rylan Patty, who was the Post’s Honorable Mention Athlete of the Month in September. “I love this team because everyone has been so welcoming,” Patty said. “No one has an ego, everyone is willing to pass and listen to input. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team continued its dominance atop the Western Alameda County Conference’s Mission Division. Last Friday, October 25, the Highlanders obliterated the visiting Washington Huskies of Fremont 56-20 at Witter Field. It wasn’t the best start after allowing the game’s opening touchdown and relinquishing a fumble on the first possession, but Piedmont jumped out to a 42-14 lead by halftime while forcing five turnovers on the night. The result improved Piedmont’s record to 7-1 overall and 3-0 against league opponents. a one-game lead over Hayward and Newark Memorial. PHS already defeated Hayward 35-14 on October 11. They will face Newark in the season-finale on November 8. “I was telling the coaches this was the most unsatisfying 50-point game. Yeah, we made plays, but we’re getting ready for playoffs and we have bigger aspirations than winning the Mission Division. We know that when we get to NCS, we can’t leave a team on the hook like we did in the first quarter tonight,” said coach Jordan Seiden. It was another big performance by Piedmont’s Xavier Henderson, who is a player that has a knack for filling the stat sheet on both offense and defense. On Saturday night, Henderson had one kickoff return for a touchdown, one twopoint reception, and had a forced fumble, fumble recovery and a tackle for loss all on one play. “I just relied on my blockers, let the play develop, and tried to turn nothing into something,” Henderson said of his long kickoff return. “On the fumble, it was one of my first blitzes of the game. I knew I had to execute and just show up when it mattered,” he added. Game Recap Piedmont led 28-7 by the end of a high-scoring first quarter and extended the gap to 42-14 by halftime. After driving down to Piedmont’s 20, linebacker Cash Elmquist blocked the Huskies’ field goal. articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi Leighton Mand, a sophomore, was second overall in a field of 71 runners at a league meet at Oyster Bay. She achieved a big personal record time. The Highlanders’ cross country team competed in its third Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season at Oyster Bay in San Leandro on Wednesday, October 23. Piedmont’s girls’ team finished second of nine schools, and the boys’ team was fourth of 10 schools. Piedmont will next compete on Saturday, November 9 in the Western Alameda County Conference Championship at Hayward High. “We have about 15 days without racing to get ready for the WACC League Championship at Hayward High. It’s an important time for recovery and training,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. For the girls’ team, it marked another strong performance by sophomore Leighton Mand, who was second overall in a field of 71 runners. Her time of 19:09.49t marked a personal record on a three-mile course, eclipsing her previous best by nearly 30 seconds after having her fastest time just four days earlier at the Wilder Mariner Invitational. Mand is having a breakout season. She was named Athlete of the Week by the Post on October 9 after leading Piedmont’s team to first place at the Artichoke Invitational in Half Moon Bay on October 5. Teammate Skylar Best, a junior, finished seventh with a time of 19:51.58 and classmate Cora Chun was 10th in 20:00.86. Freshman Viviane Oesterer was 11th in 20:07.37,and junior Cora Brozowski Schrader rounded out Piedmont’s top five with a 17th place finish in 20:37.06. Boys results Sophomore Sebastien Swain led the way once again, placing 10th of 91 runners with a time of 16:55.2. Behind Swain was junior Noah Sohn, clocking a time of 17:07.32 to finish 17th. Sophomore Alex Schleuning was 20th in 17:14.57, sophomore Thomas Ero was 27th in 17:29.58, and senior Oliver Horsley was 29th in 17:34.51. NEXT UP Piedmont goes to Hayward High for the 2024 WACC Cross Country Championship on Saturday, November 9. The varsity boys race starts at 12:00 p.m., and varsity girls at 12:30 p.m. Cora Chun finished her race in 10th place, helping Piedmont claim second place. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. articles.text: The California Symphony will showcase the crowning achievements of a composer at the peak of his powers with “Brahms Odyssey” this Saturday, November 2 at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday, November 3 at 4 p.m. in Walnut Creek. The program, conducted by Donato Cabrera, will open with Benjamin Britten’s lively Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, which uses a memorable theme to introduce different instruments in the orchestra, taking listeners on a journey through the strings, woodwinds, percussion, brass and more. Former California Symphony Resident Composer Mason Bates will invoke the spirit of Disney’s classic Fantasia in his Grammy-winning concerto for orchestra and animated film, Philharmonia Fantastique: The Making of the Orchestra. The program will close with Johannes Brahms’ Symphony No. 4, a deeply emotional, poignant masterpiece from the eminent composer. It was the last symphony he wrote, and many consider it to be the pinnacle of his career. “In choosing Benjamin Britten’s Young Person’s Guide to the Donato Cabrera will conduct a California Symphony program this Saturday and Sunday featuring Brahms’ Symphony No. 4, preceded by two colorfully imaginative orchestral pieces for young listeners. Orchestra and Bates’s Philharmonia Fantastique, we will be performing two works that belong to a long tradition of works composed to showcase the incredibly powerful sounds that only the instruments of the orchestra can produce,” Cabrera added. Britten’s guide piece was commissioned in 1945 for a British documentary film, Instruments of the Orchestra with the London Symphony Orchestra. Philharmonia Fantastique is a multi-media concerto from Mason Bates and award-winning filmmakers Gary Rydstrom and Jim Capobianco. Fantastique, like Britten’s Guide, is a tour through the orchestra – this time paired with an animated film guided by a magical young character, Sprite, whose curiosity leads a vibrant dive into the makings of an orchestra and the inner workings of its instruments. This imaginative piece won a Grammy Award in 2023. Tickets ($25-$95) for the concerts at the Lesher Center for the Arts’ Hofmann Theatre (1601 Civic Drive, Walnut Creek) are available online at californiasymphony.org, or by phone at 925- 943-7469.

articles.text: The Left Coast Chamber Ensemble presents Pierrot Lunaire, a concert of genre-breaking works from the 20th century, in two concerts this weekend. On Saturday, November 2, they will perform at 7:30 p.m. at Noe Valley Ministry in San Francisco, with a repeat concert on Sunday at 4 p.m. at the Hillside Club in Berkeley. The two concerts open the Ensemble’s 2024-25 season, and will feature Arnold Schoenberg’s melodrama opus Pierrot Lunaire. In honor of the late composer’s 150th birthday, conductor Nikki Einfeld will bring a theatrical flair to the role. Schoenberg has been long recognized not only for his invention of the twelve-tone technique but also for the extraordinary range of his compositional skill. Pierrot Lunaire is one of his most celebrated works, setting 21 selected poems from writer Albert Giraud’s cycle of the same name that explores the gamut of human emotion, from nostalgia to gallows humor. Listeners will enjoy a concert experience which combines theater, cabaret and avant-garde music. “This program exists in an atmosphere where melancholy and humor co-exist, The atmosphere is amplified by the intimacy of two of the Bay Area’s most enchanting small venues,” said Left Coast Chamber Ensemble Artistic Director Matilda Hofman. The performances will take place at Noe Valley Ministry (1021 Sanchez Street, San Francisco) and the Hillside Club (2286 Cedar Street, Berkeley). Tickets ($35 in advance, $38 at the door; $15 students in advance, $18 students at the door) may be bought online leftcoastensemble. org/pierrot, by phone at 415-617- 5223 or at the door. Enjoy a performance of Pierrot Lunaire spanning poetry, music and the human voice as the Left Coast Chamber Ensemble performs in San Francisco this Saturday and in Berkeley on Sunday.

articles.text: Grammy-nominated group to highlight American Indian songs, Dvorˇák Cal Performances will welcome the Dover Quartet this Sunday, November 3, for a 3 p.m. concert ar Hertz Hall exploring the cultural traditions that shape American concert music. The twice-Grammy-nominated ensemble will perform the West Coast premiere of Emmy-winning American Indian composer Jerod Tate’s new work Abokkoli’ Taloowa (“Woodland Songs”), co-commissioned by Cal Performances, om addition to Tate’s arrangement of Rattle Songs by Indigenous composer Pura Fé. Dvořák’s renowned American Quartet and composer Jessie Montgomery’s string piece Strum round out the program. The performance is part of Cal Performances’ “Illuminations: Fractured History” series of programs for the 2024–25 season. “The program illuminates and expands the robust connections between many American voices, including jazz, bluegrass, Indigenous American music and Western classical music. articles.text: Italians invented the scenario and the word. It entered the American vernacular. The story is fascinating. Giuseppe Tartini (1692-1770) was the most important violinist of his generation. He was also a great swordsman and a famous lover. Our story begins with love. Tartini was in love with the daughter of a wealthy man. The girl’s father not only objected to the marriage, he wanted to kill Tartini. Hearing of the plot to kill him, Tartini fled his city and took refuge in a monastery. Night after night, he had the same dream. It was his desire to become the greatest violinist in the world. In his dream, he makes a pact with the devil – a timeless story. Tartiini would become the greatest violinist, but he must relinquish his soul to the devil. At the last minute, Tartini questions, the honesty of the Lord of darkness. He challenges the devil to demonstrate his ability to play the violin…and the devil does just that! In the dream, the devil performs the most beautiful and difficult music on the violin. Tartini said afterward, that he was unable to breathe, so beautiful was the devil’s music. Night after night, he attempted to write on paper the music of his dream. The result was “The Devil’s Trill Sonata,” certainly Tartini’s most famous composition, and without a doubt his greatest. It begins with a dreamlike introduction. In the second movement, the music becomes more agitated with the violinist conversing with the devil. In the third movement, we hear the extraordinary devil’s trill. The Sonata comes to a dramatic conclusion with a florid cadenza for the solo violin played with continuous trills. And then the orchestra joins in a triumphant finale. This composition is certainly one of the monuments in all of music. Almost parallel to the story of Tartini is the story of another Baroque composer, Alessandro Stradella. He was in love with a mistress of a Venetian Senator. To save themselves, they fled to Rome. Stradella’s musical career flourished and his music was performed everywhere. Two assassins were engaged to murder Stradella. They attended a performance of one of Stradella’s compositions and intended to murder him afterwards. They were overcome by the beauty of the music and instead of murdering him they told him that his life was in danger and allowed him to escape unharmed. Once again, the young couple fled and came under the protection of the Duchess of Savoy. articles.text: Catch the Olivier Award-winning comedy The Play That Goes Wrong before it closes at the San Francisco Playhouse with a final performance this Saturday. This fast-paced farce filled with slapstick silliness finds the bumbling Cornley Polytechnic Drama Society on the opening night of its newest production, “The Murder of Haversham.” As the incompetent theatre troupe attempts to stage this 1920s murder mystery, their production devolves into madcap mayhem. Lost props, forgotten lines and poorly constructed scenery conspire against the clumsy cast, who fight for the show to go on as they struggle to survive until the final curtain call. Written by London’s Mischief Theatre co-founders Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer and Henry Shields, The Play That Goes Wrong was performed for nearly a decade in London’s West End, winning the Olivier Award for Best New Comedy before moving to Broadway. The New York Times deemed it a “gut-busting hit. One of those breakneck exercises in idiocy that make you laugh till you cry. It starts off punch-drunk and just keeps getting drunker.” San Francisco Playhouse co-founder Susi Damilano directs this hilarious whodunit. Tickets ($63-$135) and showtimes for performances at SF Playhouse (450 Post St.) are available at sfplayhouse.org/sfph/ get-tickets.

articles.text: The Edge of Seventeen is superb. It is certainly one of the best movies about adolescent angst and coming of age in the last 25 years. It’s that good. To write and direct a film that captures the essence of being 17 is no small thing. It’s a time when your life is unmoored and uncertain, a time when you’re feeling at a loss to understand your emotions. Director Kelly Fremon Craig gets it just right, avoiding a minefield of clichés. At the center of Edge is Nadine (Hailee Steinfeld), suffering with a perfect storm of emotions. Several years ago she lost her father, to whom she was especially close. And now her best friend since childhood, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has fallen for her older, eternally perfect and popular brother, Darian (Blake Jenner). Nadine feels abruptly rejected and betrayed and so banishes Krista from her life. Suddenly rudderless, friendless, and convinced she is utterly alone, she decides to kill herself (or imagines she will, more concept that anything approaching reality). During lunch hour she informs Mr. Bruner (a remarkably good Woody Harrelson), her history teacher, of her intention. While Nadine is a master of histrionics and self-absorbed drama, the laconic and dry Mr. Bruner becomes the perfect counterweight to her grandiose mood swings. articles.text: Though the film Suffragette takes place more than 100 years ago (1912-1913), and though its core issue – a woman’s right to vote – has long ago been settled, the narrative still feels contemporary and relevant. A century has indeed passed, yet we know that women today still struggle for equal pay and job opportunities and, of course, the ongoing debate regarding the ultimate control of their bodies. What has been dimmed by the passage of time are the harrowing risks women took as they did battle with an iron-fisted, often misogynistic patriarchy that was committed to preventing them from acquiring the right to vote. The story is told through the eyes of Maud Watts (Carey Mulligan), an English working class woman, who works 12-hour days in a large factory-like laundry, washing and ironing other people’s clothes. In act one, Maud, who leads an insulated, narrow life – she’s married and has a son – is terrified when she finds herself on a London street and is unexpectedly swept up in a demonstration by suffragettes who are insisting on the right to vote. Suddenly Maud finds herself surrounded by women who are prepared to confront the police, feel the pain of their clubs, and endure arrest and weeks of incarceration for a cause in which they passionately believe. These courageous women are a revelation to Maud. She has long felt oppressed and treated as if she were mere property to be used and then disposed of by men. Abruptly the scales fall from her eyes and her consciousness is raised. Against all of her instincts, against everything she has been told about her place in the world (repeatedly by her husband), she rebels and joins what soon becomes a rising tide of civil disobedience, meaning destruction of property. In one moving moment in the film, Maud sits in front of government officials and describes her work and life and finally says quietly, “There might be another way of living this life.” That other way comes at great cost and personal pain. She discovers that the government is capable of remorseless harm: the suffragettes are beaten, jailed, and force-fed. As well, their neighbors (and society at large), voice their disapprobation by shunning and ridiculing them. Maud didn’t know that she would be asked to sacrifice all that she once held dear; but that is exactly the price that is exacted. Suffragette tells a powerful story. articles.text: Reese Witherspoon, Oprah Winfrey, Zach Galifianakis, Mindy Kaling, Storm Reid, Levi Miller, and Deric McCabe in A Wrinkle in Time If you have some youngsters hanging around the house, well, find A Wrinkle in Time. It’s a gorgeous film, a solid adventure, and will easily touch their sense of wonder. As an adult I acknowledge that the most interesting part of the story for me was the beginning when Meg Murry (Storm Reid) is introduced. She’s a 13-year-old middle schooler who has developed an attitude that gets her either picked on by her school’s Mean Girls or results in a visit to the principle’s office. In truth Meg has been grieving since the baffling disappearance four years ago of her beloved father, Dr. Alex Murry (Chris Pine), a physicist. Meg is clearly gifted, though she suffers from a damaged self-image and sense of self-worth. Her mother (Gugu Mbatha-Raw), who’s also a physicist, is equally devastated by the loss of her husband, and is upset with Meg. It’s only Meg’s brother, Charles Wallace (Deric McCabe), who is convinced some new friends can assist them in finding their father. As it turns out, Calvin, from Meg’s school, shows up one day and is around when Charles’ new acquaintances reveal themselves: Mrs. Which (Oprah Winfrey), Mrs. Whatsit (Reese Witherspoon) and Mrs. Who (Mindy Kaling). They are celestial, ephemeral beings that agree to help Meg and Charles Wallace and Calvin find Dr. Murry. And so off they go, into the farthest parts of the universe. It’s quite a journey and one that first introduces the kids to a planet of light. It’s there that they confront the IT, which represents the dark side of life – a threatening essence that the three must face alone and likely has Meg’s father. Mrs. Which tells them that IT is spreading through the universe and to be careful. Remember, this is a kids’ movie and therefore has as its premise a complete suspension of disbelief. An example is the word “tessering,” meaning a wrinkle in time and the way that the three Mrs. and Meg, et al. travel across the universe. It proves to be a great trip (and back), filled with lessons for all of them. Older kids will enjoy A Wrinkle in Time, especially tweens and newbie teens. A Wrinkle in Time. Directed by Ava DuVernay. articles.text: It was a beautiful fall morning last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays group. Halloween was just a week away, so they decided to see some Halloween house decorations. A large turnout of 48 walkers and four K-9 best friends were on hand for the fun. Before last week’s walk, some history was shared. Halloween’s origins date back to the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain (pronounced sow-in) when people lit bonfires and wore costumes to ward off ghosts. The Celts, who lived 2,000 years ago mostly in what is now Ireland, the UK and northern France, celebrated their new year on November 1. This day marked the end of summer and the harvest, and the beginning of the dark, cold winter. It was a time of year often associated with death. Celts believed that on the night before the new year, the boundary between the worlds of the living and the dead became blurred. On the night of October 31, they celebrated Samhain, when they believed ghosts returned to earth. The people built huge, sacred bonfires to burn crops and animals as sacrifices to their Celtic gods. During the celebration, the Celts wore costumes, typically consisting of animal heads and skins. had conquered most of the Celtic territory. During the 400 years they ruled they combined their Roman festivals with the Samhain celebration. In the eighth century, Pope Gregory III designated November 1 as a time to honor all saints. Soon, All Saints Day also incorporated some Samhain traditions. The evening was known as All Hallows Eve, and later became known simply as Hallowe’en (Hallloween). Over time, Halloween evolved into a day of activities like trickor-treating, carving jack-o-lanterns, wearing costumes, and eating treats. However, it was not until after the mass Irish and Scottish immigrations in the 19th century that Halloween became a major American holiday. With this new understanding of Halloween, the walkers went down Magnolia Avenue in search of ghosts and goblins. Sherry Jacobs led them to a front yard she thought the group would enjoy. It had headstones for family cats with funny names, and a “Cat Crossing” sign attached to the back of a city street sign. The walkers went to Dracena Avenue, now famous for its annual tradition of transforming the block-long street into Sleepy Hallow, with small, white ghosts hanging from trees all along the street. On Park Way and on Blair the group found a two-story, inflatable, black cat. Them it was over to Sheridan and Lincoln and Crocker Avenue. The front yard of a house on Crocker had been transformed into a fully occupied graveyard with headstones, ghouls emerging from their graves, huge spiders, a ghost clown swinging from a tree. By chance, the notscary owner of the house, Peter Wagener, was unloading his car, so he stopped to tell the walkers how his family had bought the house three years ago. Each year they create a spooktacular show for trick or treaters. About 350 brave ones got full size candy bars last year. Peter said his dentist, a brother-in-law, voiced no objections. It proved to be a great spot for a group photo with Peter and his other-world friends. There were more yards to see on Sea View Avenue, but time had run out, so they returned to the Exedra after a good long walk with lots of Halloween fun. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Osh, Oakland Zoo’s male African elephant bull and the zoo’s last African elephant, successful moved cross country to settle into his new home on October 18 at The Elephant Sanctuary in Tennessee. Oakland Zoo Animal Care Team members and a Zoo Veterinarian accompanied Osh on the 46-hour road trip to Tennessee where he joins six female African elephants and a prospective male companion named Artie. With Osh’s move, the Oakland Zoo will be without elephants for the first time in 75 years. This provides the opportunity for the zoo to reimagine the future of the elephant habitat. The zoo will have to renovate the 35-year-old habitat, including the barn and behind-the-scenes areas. The zoo announced Osh’s departure in July and plans for him to relocate to The Elephant Sanctuary. This decision was made due to The Sanctuary’s unwavering commitment to animal care and wellbeing, and their ability to provide a suitable home catering to his companionship needs. Moving an elephant is challenging, and several things needed to be done before Osh was cleared to move across the country. Osh’s Animal Care Team worked with him several times a week through voluntary training to help him get used to his custom air-conditioned trailer, which was built to accommodate his 15,000 pound weight and 11’2” height. Osh’s keepers described him as highly adaptable, calm, and resilient. The Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital staff conducted foot and tusk radiographs, blood tests, and physical and visual exams. When loaded onto his trailer last Wednesday morning, he was prepared and healthy for his move to Tennessee. The journey to Tennessee was smooth, according to zoo officials, and Osh remained calm throughout. The team, consisting of two of Osh’s Oakland Zoo animal care keepers and an Oakland Zoo veterinarian, stopped every three hours to check on Osh and feed him. He ate celery, beet pulp, and watermelons – lots of watermelons – during the trip. The team also monitored him closely with cameras in his trailer. After the long journey he joyfully began clearing trees, eating, and roaming through his new habitat. “After only a few days at The Sanctuary, he continues to be a rambunctious and resilient being, joyfully exploring his new habitat. My heart is so full seeing Osh at his new forever home,” said Gina Kinzley, Zoological Manager at Oakland Zoo. The dedicated care team at The Sanctuary visited Osh in Oakland in August this year to get to know him better, learn about Oakland Zoo’s elephant program, and deepen their understanding of the strong relationship they have built over 20 years. articles.text: Fifteen members of the Piedmont Seniors group attended a performance of the screwball comedy Arsenic and Old Lace at the Lesher Theatre of the Arts in downtown Walnut Creek on September 21. This enduring show is a wacky makeover by Matt Morrow making his Center REP directorial debut. Mortimer Brewster (Cody Sloan), who lives with his two elderly spinster aunts, Martha and Abby Brewster (humorously portrayed by Michael Patrick Gaffney and Danny Scheie), discovers that they are harboring some killer secrets, just as his estranged brother descends upon the family home, upending everything he thought to be true in his life. The two aunts had poisoned some boarders and then hid them in the basement of their lodging house. To save his family and his own sanity, Mortimer, who works as a theater critic and is dating Elaine, the daughter of the minister who lives next door, must learn to navigate a new world gone mad. What follows is funny and the audience tries to navigate how the sisters will manage to redeem themselves from these murders. Many of the other characters also play roles of the opposite sex, which is a hilarious take on this classic comedy. The laughs are too numerous to count, and the performances are strong from top to bottom. Center Rep’s version of this classic offers a new vision for one of theater’s most enduring comedies. After the show the Seniors headed to a nearby Thai restaurant, Andaman. Though some of the Seniors were a little reluctant to try a new style of Asian food, they enjoyed the flavors of this terrific restaurant. Several members commented that this restaurant served the best drinks they had ever tasted. The service was superb and the wait staff was very eager to please. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors prepare to begin a guided tour of Safari West. Pictured are: Peggy Rourke (left), Nava Shaham, Mona Jamieson, Gloria Wilmer, Carole Jones, Nancy Hinsch, Lois Horwitz, Susan McCreary, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Tanya Hu, Jim Ayotte, and Larry Hu. The Piedmont Seniors group recently put on their collective safari hats and ventured north to Santa Rosa for a tour of Safari West, a 400-acre wildlife refuge preserve and home to over 800 animals representing the biodiversity of Africa. The Seniors hopped on a rugged safari truck as they made their way through the park. Animals seen on the tour included ostriches, monkeys, antelope, rhinos, cheetahs, steer, bulls, flamingos, and giraffes. Some of the animals were even on the endangered list. The Seniors learned that the taller giraffes’ tongues could extend to 17 inches and that they eat for up to 10 hours during the day. One of the highlights was seeing the Watusi cattle with large horns casually lounging together. After a tour on the Safari truck, the Seniors split into two groups and had a guided walking tour, allowing them to get close to many of the birds, including cranes, ducks, geese, guinea fowl, hornbills, and flamingos. Following the walking tour the group had lunch at Safari West’s Savannah Café, sharing an experience inspired by the legendary South African Braai (pronounced “bry”). This outdoor buffet, with an American barbecue tradition, featured a feast of culinary creations that appealed to everyone. Then it was time for the group to visit Safari West’s wonderful gift shop, which offers a number of interesting items for purchase including gemstones, jewelry, and apparel. They even sell huge ostrich eggs. The group was fortunate to be able to visit the park as the disastrous Tubbs fire in 2017 did enormous damage to the surrounding area. Safari West’s owner lost his home and vehicles while trying to save the animals. No animal was lost in the terrible fire. Safari West invites visitors to stay overnight in its comfortable tent cabins. Though the tents are comfortable with necessary amenities, be aware that the animals can get a little noisy during the nighttime hours. Binoculars and cameras are encouraged throughout the park. This park is suitable for people of all ages, and its purpose is to conserve the animals. Reservations are required to visit Safari West. It is the closest you can get to Africa without a passport! For more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, in addition to monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, October 30, 2024 Seniors Piedmont Seniors get taste of Africa – in Sonoma County Piedmont Seniors revisit a classic at Lesher Theatre of the Arts By Janet Epstein Fifteen members of the Piedmont Seniors group attended a performance of the screwball comedy Arsenic and Old Lace at the Lesher Theatre of the Arts in downtown Walnut Creek on September 21. This enduring show is a wacky makeover by Matt Morrow making his Center REP directorial debut. Mortimer Brewster (Cody Sloan), who lives with his two elderly spinster aunts, Martha and Abby Brewster (humorously portrayed by Michael Patrick Gaffney and Danny Scheie), discovers that they are harboring some killer secrets, just as his estranged brother descends upon the family home, upending everything he thought to be true in his life. The two aunts had poisoned some boarders and then hid them in the basement of their lodging house. To save his family and his own sanity, Mortimer, who works as a theater critic and is dating Elaine, the daughter of the minister who lives next door, must learn to navigate a new world gone mad. What follows is funny and the audience tries to navigate how the sisters will manage to redeem themselves from these murders. Many of the other characters also play roles of the opposite sex, which is a hilarious take on this classic comedy. The laughs are too numerous to count, and the performances are strong from top to bottom. Center Rep’s version of this classic offers a new vision for one of theater’s most enduring comedies. After the show the Seniors headed to a nearby Thai restaurant, Andaman. Though some of the Seniors were a little reluctant to try a new style of Asian food, they enjoyed the flavors of this terrific restaurant. Several members commented that this restaurant served the best drinks they had ever tasted. The service was superb and the wait staff was very eager to please. The Piedmont Seniors prepare to begin a guided tour of Safari West. Pictured are: Peggy Rourke (left), Nava Shaham, Mona Jamieson, Gloria Wilmer, Carole Jones, Nancy Hinsch, Lois Horwitz, Susan McCreary, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Tanya Hu, Jim Ayotte, and Larry Hu. The Piedmont Seniors group recently put on their collective safari hats and ventured north to Santa Rosa for a tour of Safari West, a 400-acre wildlife refuge preserve and home to over 800 animals representing the biodiversity of Africa. The Seniors hopped on a rugged safari truck as they made their way through the park. Animals seen on the tour included ostriches, monkeys, antelope, rhinos, cheetahs, steer, bulls, flamingos, and giraffes. Some of the animals were even on the endangered list. The Seniors learned that the taller giraffes’ tongues could extend to 17 inches and that they eat for up to 10 hours during the day. One of the highlights was seeing the Watusi cattle with large horns casually lounging together. After a tour on the Safari truck, the Seniors split into two groups and had a guided walking tour, allowing them to get close to many of the birds, including cranes, ducks, geese, guinea fowl, hornbills, and flamingos. Following the walking tour the group had lunch at Safari West’s Savannah Café, sharing an experience inspired by the legendary South African Braai (pronounced “bry”). This outdoor buffet, with an American barbecue tradition, featured a feast of culinary creations that appealed to everyone. Then it was time for the group to visit Safari West’s wonderful gift shop, which offers a number of interesting items for purchase including gemstones, jewelry, and apparel. They even sell huge ostrich eggs. The group was fortunate to be able to visit the park as the disastrous Tubbs fire in 2017 did enormous damage to the surrounding area. Safari West’s owner lost his home and vehicles while trying to save the animals. No animal was lost in the terrible fire. Safari West invites visitors to stay overnight in its comfortable tent cabins. Though the tents are comfortable with necessary amenities, be aware that the animals can get a little noisy during the nighttime hours. Binoculars and cameras are encouraged throughout the park. This park is suitable for people of all ages, and its purpose is to conserve the animals. Reservations are required to visit Safari West. It is the closest you can get to Africa without a passport! For more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, in addition to monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. articles.text: Editor: Several years ago, there was a proposal to build a soccer field at Moraga Canyon. At the time, many of us were opposed to the idea based on our research of 33 species of wildlife who lived in Moraga Canyon. Now again, there is a proposed idea to build nearly 200 housing units near the corporation yard and across the street as well. Once again we are opposed to this idea. The species of wildlife in the Canyon would be completely displaced by this project. I understand that this proposal also includes a traffic signal that will snarl traffic along Moraga Way.
